passage:
Sunday night
Dear Diary,
Science project is due tomorrow. On Friday I told Mumma it would take ten minutes, just a volcano with baking soda. Easy!
But first I couldn't find the clay. Then Nazia didi was using the glue. Then my volcano fell over twice because the bottle was too tall. It's ten o'clock now and it's still wet and brown and sad.
Mumma said, "My boy and his ten minutes." She reminded me that with the solar system model I also said ten minutes, and we were up till eleven. I forgot all about that. Every time, I think it will be quick. Next time I'm starting on Friday. Maybe.
Tavish

qa.q: What kept making Tavish's volcano fall over?
qa.a: It fell over twice because the bottle was too tall.

qa.q: Why did Tavish think the project would take ten minutes?
qa.a: Tavish felt confident because he pictured only the easy volcano and forgot the solar system model, when he also said ten minutes and was up till eleven.

qa.q: What could Tavish try for the next project?
qa.a: He could remember how long the last one took, gather the clay and glue early, and really start on Friday.

qa.q: What is Sunday night like for Mumma?
qa.a: Mumma is up late with a wet volcano she saw coming, since the same thing happened with the solar system model.

grounding: A boy expects his volcano project to take ten minutes and starts the night before, forgetting his last project ran late.

passage: In Kainakary, where every house faces the canal, Thomas had two weeks to make a leaf album for his EVS class: twenty different leaves, pressed and labelled. "Easy. One evening," he told his friend Noor as they fished off the jetty. Every evening after that there was cricket, or fishing, or the ferry to watch. On the last night Thomas ran around the compound with a torch, pulling leaves off the jackfruit and banana trees. The coconut leaf was too big to press. The hibiscus leaves curled in the heat of the lamp. Half the names he didn't know. At eleven, Ammachi found him asleep on the verandah beside twelve crumpled leaves. It was exactly what had happened with his shell collection last term, though he hadn't thought of it once.

qa.q: How many leaves did the album need?
qa.a: Twenty different leaves, pressed and labelled.

qa.q: Why did Thomas say it would take one evening?
qa.a: Thomas felt confident because he pictured the smooth version of the task and never thought of his shell collection last term, so it felt easy.

qa.q: What small step could have helped Thomas in the first week?
qa.a: He could have collected a few leaves each evening before fishing or cricket, so the last night wasn't a scramble.

qa.q: How might Ammachi feel finding Thomas asleep on the verandah?
qa.a: Ammachi may feel tender and a bit worried, seeing him worn out beside only twelve crumpled leaves.

grounding: A boy thinks a two-week leaf album will take one evening and scrambles the night before, having forgotten a similar delay.

passage: On Sunday evening in their Berlin apartment block, Pablo knocked on Zeynep's door. "Can I borrow your coloured pencils? My castle poster is due tomorrow." Zeynep's eyes went wide. "You said it would take half an hour. That was three weeks ago." "It will take half an hour," Pablo said. "Draw the castle, write three facts, done." Back home, he spent forty minutes on the drawbridge alone. Then he couldn't find the book with the castle facts. Then his little brother spilled juice on one corner. At ten, his father found him close to tears with only the towers finished. "Remember the dinosaur poster?" his father said softly. Pablo did, now. That one was going to take half an hour too.

qa.q: What did Pablo ask to borrow from Zeynep?
qa.a: He asked to borrow her coloured pencils.

qa.q: Why was Pablo sure the poster would take half an hour?
qa.a: Pablo felt confident because he imagined only 'draw the castle, write three facts, done', and didn't think of the dinosaur poster that had also run late. 😔

qa.q: What would you advise Pablo for his next poster?
qa.a: Think back to how long the dinosaur poster really took, start weeks earlier, and do one part at a time.

qa.q: How might Zeynep see Pablo's plan?
qa.a: Zeynep remembers his 'half an hour' from three weeks ago, so she can see the trouble coming more clearly than he can.

grounding: A boy believes a poster will take half an hour, starts the night before, and only then remembers a similar project.

Keerthana: ok plan: whole chem syllabus this weekend. 14 chapters, 7 a day. easy 💪

qa.q: How many chapters had Keerthana done by Sunday evening?

qa.q: How does Keerthana feel on Sunday evening, and why?

qa.q: Which part of Sahil's reply helps, and why?

qa.q: How does Sahil see the plan from the start?
qa.a: Sahil remembers the day Keerthana managed only 3 bio chapters, so the 7-a-day plan looks unrealistic to Sahil right away.

grounding: A teenager plans the whole chemistry syllabus in one weekend, ignores past experience, and is shocked when it takes far longer.

passage: In Ottapalam, the board exam timetable was taped to the steel almirah in Gopika's room. On Friday evening she drew a neat plan: all of history on Saturday, all of geography on Sunday. "Two days, whole syllabus," she told Arnab, whose family had moved from Kolkata and who lived across the paddy field. "I'm faster than people think." Arnab, who'd heard her say this before the half-yearly exam, said nothing. Saturday brought a power cut, a visiting aunt, and the chapter on the freedom movement, which alone took till dinner. By Sunday night she had covered four history chapters out of eleven and not opened geography. She sat staring at the timetable, honestly stunned. How could it be this slow? She had been so sure.

qa.q: Where was the timetable taped?
qa.a: The timetable was taped to the steel almirah in Gopika's room.

qa.q: Why was Gopika so stunned on Sunday night?
qa.a: She had pictured a smooth weekend where she was faster than people think, so four chapters out of eleven came as a shock.

qa.q: What could Gopika do differently before the next exam?
qa.a: She could check how long her half-yearly revision really took and spread the plan over more days, with room for power cuts and visitors.

qa.q: Why might Arnab have said nothing when he heard the plan?
qa.a: Arnab had heard the same before the half-yearly exam, so he may have doubted it but didn't want to discourage her.

grounding: A teenager plans to revise two whole subjects in a weekend and is stunned when one chapter takes a whole day.

passage: Chen had the whole spring break mapped out on the whiteboard in his Vancouver bedroom. Monday: all of algebra. Tuesday: all of geometry. Wednesday: statistics, then free days. "Exams are in two weeks. I'll be done by Wednesday and gaming by Thursday," he told Oskar over the phone. Oskar laughed. "You said that at Christmas." "Christmas was different. My cousins were visiting." By Wednesday night, Chen was still on algebra. Every practice set took twice as long as the answers at the back made it look. On Thursday morning he stared at the whiteboard, marker in hand, feeling almost betrayed by it. Three topics, one done. He wiped off 'free days' and started again, with Oskar's Christmas warning ringing in his ears.

qa.q: What was Chen still on by Wednesday night?
qa.a: By Wednesday night, Chen was still on algebra.

qa.q: Why did Chen feel almost betrayed by the whiteboard?
qa.a: He had trusted the bright picture on it, and real work taking twice as long felt like the plan had let him down.

qa.q: How could Chen build a more realistic plan now?
qa.a: He could time one practice set, use that to estimate the rest, and remember how Christmas actually went before writing new days.

qa.q: What would change if Chen had listened to Oskar's Christmas reminder?
qa.a: He might have planned fewer topics a day from the start and avoided Thursday's shock.

grounding: A teenager maps a whole maths syllabus into three days, ignores his Christmas experience, and is shocked when algebra alone fills all three.

passage: Yuki had to be out of her Osaka dormitory by noon on Saturday. On Wednesday, Olga asked if she wanted help packing. "It's one room," Yuki said. "Friday afternoon, three hours, done." Friday afternoon arrived with a seminar that ran late. The boxes she'd planned to pick up from the supermarket were gone. Her books alone filled six bags, and the rice cooker wouldn't fit anywhere. At midnight the floor was still covered in clothes and cables, and the dorm office had already sent a reminder about the noon inspection. Yuki sat on her bare mattress and texted Olga, hands shaking: "Are you awake? I thought it was one room." Olga arrived at seven with tape and coffee, and they worked until the last minute.

qa.q: By what time did Yuki have to be out of the dormitory?
qa.a: By noon on Saturday.

qa.q: How did Yuki feel at midnight, and what shows it?
qa.a: She was panicking; her hands were shaking as she texted Olga, 'I thought it was one room.' 😰

qa.q: What could Yuki have done on Wednesday?
qa.a: She could have accepted Olga's help and started earlier, allowing for things like a late seminar or missing boxes.

qa.q: What is it like for Olga to get the midnight text?
qa.a: Olga, who had offered help days before, probably felt concerned and still turned up at seven with tape and coffee.

grounding: A student thinks moving out will take three hours and panics the night before the deadline.

passage: In the physics department's basement lab, a paper calendar hung above Nilesh's desk with THESIS DUE circled in red on the 30th. In March he'd told his guide, Dr Bose, "I'll write it in two weeks. The experiments are done; it's just typing." Gurleen, at the next bench, had offered to swap chapter drafts early. He'd waved it off. Now it was the 24th. The references were a mess, two graphs needed redoing, and the printer on the second floor had been broken for three days. At 2 am Nilesh was still in the lab, heart racing, rewriting the methods chapter for the third time. Gurleen came in to check her samples and found him staring at the red circle. "Two weeks," he said hoarsely. "I really thought two weeks."

qa.q: Which chapter was Nilesh rewriting at 2 am?
qa.a: He was rewriting the methods chapter for the third time.

qa.q: Why did Nilesh believe the thesis was 'just typing'?
qa.a: Nilesh felt confident with the experiments done, so he pictured a smooth write-up and didn't imagine messy references, graphs to redo or a broken printer.

qa.q: What could Nilesh do even now, six days out?
qa.a: He could list what's left, ask Dr Bose which parts matter most, and take up Gurleen's offer to swap drafts.

qa.q: How might Gurleen feel finding Nilesh at 2 am?
qa.a: Gurleen may feel sympathetic, and perhaps a little sad that her early offer was waved off.

grounding: A student expects to write his thesis in two weeks, waves off early help, and panics days before the deadline.

passage:
Tushar,
Please don't say "I told you so." You did, but please don't.
The scholarship application closes Friday at 5 pm. On Monday I thought it was a two-hour job: fill the form, attach marks, done. You asked if I'd started the essay and I said I'd write it Thursday night, easy.
Tuesday I found out I need an attested marksheet. The college office attests only on Wednesdays, and the queue went down the corridor. Wednesday night I realised the essay has three separate questions, not one. Today, Thursday, my referee's email bounced.
It's 11 pm. My chest is tight, one essay is half done, and I keep thinking: this is exactly what happened with the hostel form last year.
Can you read my draft tomorrow morning?
Omkar

qa.q: When does the scholarship application close?
qa.a: It closes Friday at 5 pm.

qa.q: What is Omkar feeling on Thursday night, and what shows it?
qa.a: Omkar is panicking: a tight chest, one essay half done, and the memory of the same mess with last year's hostel form.

qa.q: What could Omkar do the next time an application opens?
qa.a: Omkar could read every requirement on day one, check office timings early, and remember how long the hostel form really took.

qa.q: How might Tushar feel reading 'Please don't say I told you so'?
qa.a: Tushar may be tempted to say it, but also feel concerned and glad to be trusted with the draft.

grounding: A student treats a scholarship application as a two-hour job and panics the night before it closes.

passage: Jyoti, a customer asks when her lehenga will be ready, and you say "Tuesday" just to please her. I did that too, at twenty-four, when I'd just opened this shop. Then I missed three weddings' worth of Tuesdays. So I started doing what my Abbu did with his carpentry orders. I opened my old register and looked: how long did the last five bridal lehengas actually take? Not how long I hoped. Eleven days, fourteen, nine, sixteen, twelve. Then I broke the work into parts: cutting, embroidery, lining, fitting. And I added three days for the things that always go wrong, like the thread shop being shut or the customer changing the neckline. After that, people started saying "Rehana's dates are real dates." So take the register. Look first, then promise.

qa.q: How long did the last five bridal lehengas take?
qa.a: Eleven days, fourteen, nine, sixteen and twelve.

qa.q: Why did Rehana start checking the old register?
qa.a: After missing three weddings' worth of Tuesdays, Rehana wanted dates based on what had really happened, not on hope.

qa.q: What steps does Rehana want Jyoti to follow before promising a date?
qa.a: Check the register for similar orders, break the job into parts, add days for what usually goes wrong, and only then give a date.

qa.q: How might customers feel once Rehana's dates became reliable?
qa.a: Customers could plan their weddings with confidence, trusting that a promised date would really be met.

grounding: An elder recalls learning, at twenty-four, to base dates on past orders, split the job into parts and add a buffer before promising.

passage: The client call was in ten minutes, and Mehak leaned over Disha's desk. "They want the new menu screens for their ordering app. Can we promise Friday?" Disha felt the pull to say yes; the team had been praised all week. Instead she opened the project log. "The last two sets of screens like this took eight and eleven working days," she said. "Design, review, the client's changes, then fixes. Each step slipped at least once." She sketched the four parts on a sticky note, gave each a number of days, and added two more for the client's usual round of edits. "Realistically, the Thursday after next. I'd rather promise that and deliver early." Mehak exhaled. "They won't love it." "They'll love a missed Friday less." Mehak took the sticky note into the call.

qa.q: How long did the last two sets of similar screens take?
qa.a: They took eight and eleven working days.

qa.q: What did Disha feel tempted to do, and why?
qa.a: Disha felt tempted to say yes to Friday because the team had been praised all week, and a quick yes would have felt pleasing in the moment.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Disha, and why?
qa.a: Checking the project log and splitting the job into four parts with two extra days gave a date built on real past work, not hope.

qa.q: How does Mehak feel about taking the later date into the call?
qa.a: Mehak is uneasy that the client won't love it, but accepts Disha's reasoning and takes the sticky note in.

grounding: Under time pressure, a worker checks past timings, breaks the job into parts and adds a buffer before promising a date.

passage: In a Ludhiana housing society, Rajni Aunty wanted her kitchen redone before Diwali. "Five weeks, beta, can you do it?" Jasleen, twenty-five and three years into running her small interiors firm, didn't answer straight away. She scrolled to the notes she kept on every job: the Malhotras' kitchen, seven weeks; the Batras', six and a half; both held up by marble delivery. She walked the kitchen with a tape measure and listed each stage on the back of a catalogue: breaking, plumbing, marble, cabinets, painting, cleaning. Next to marble she wrote "plus one week, always." "Honestly, Aunty, seven weeks. If we start Monday, it's done a week before Diwali, not the night before." Rajni Aunty frowned, then nodded. "Better than half a kitchen on Diwali."

qa.q: How long did the Malhotras' kitchen take?
qa.a: The Malhotras' kitchen took seven weeks.

qa.q: Why didn't Jasleen answer Rajni Aunty straight away?
qa.a: She wanted to check what past jobs really took before promising, rather than say what the aunty hoped to hear.

qa.q: Why is 'plus one week, always' next to marble a smart note?
qa.a: Marble delivery held up both past kitchens, so that extra week protects the promise from the step most likely to slip.

qa.q: How does Rajni Aunty come to accept the longer estimate?
qa.a: She frowns at first, then decides a finished kitchen a week before Diwali beats half a kitchen on Diwali.

grounding: A young interiors contractor checks past jobs, lists each stage and adds a buffer before promising a date.

passage: Mahima, you run a team now, so here's the thing I wish someone had told me. When I became lead at the app studio, every developer gave me dates like "Thursday, easy." And every Thursday slid to the next Tuesday. My first instinct was: they're lazy, or they don't care. But I'm Deepak, I was a developer for years, and I did exactly the same thing. It isn't laziness. It's how people picture work: the smooth version, no bugs, no meetings. So I changed two things. I ask for a range now: best case, likely case, worst case. And every month we put last month's estimates next to what really happened. No blame, just numbers. Our dates are still hopeful. But they're hopeful with their eyes open.

qa.q: What does Deepak ask for now instead of a single date?
qa.a: Deepak asks for a range: best case, likely case, worst case.

qa.q: Why did Deepak stop thinking the developers were lazy?
qa.a: Remembering doing exactly the same thing as a developer, Deepak saw the rosy dates as how people picture work, not as not caring.

qa.q: Why does the monthly comparison help, on top of the ranges?
qa.a: Putting last month's estimates next to what really happened, without blame, lets everyone learn how far off they usually are.

qa.q: How might the developers feel about the new approach?
qa.a: They'd likely feel less judged, since slipping dates are treated as a shared habit to fix, not proof of laziness.

grounding: A team lead explains seeing repeated optimistic dates as ordinary human thinking, then asking for ranges and reviewing past accuracy.

passage: I'm Anupama, the newest engineer on Keerthana's team at the bridge-design firm. In my first month I watched Sahil promise the load calculations "by Friday" three weeks in a row. Each Monday he looked a bit more embarrassed. I expected Keerthana to snap. She didn't. At the team meeting she pinned up a chart of everyone's estimates from last quarter beside the actual finish dates. Almost every bar was late, hers included. "This isn't about any one of us," she said. "Our brains picture the clean version." From then on she asked each of us for two dates: the day it's likely, and the day it's almost certain. I can't say what Sahil felt. But the next time he gave a date, he gave two, and he hit the second one.

qa.q: What did Keerthana pin up at the team meeting?
qa.a: A chart of everyone's estimates from last quarter beside the actual finish dates.

qa.q: What does Keerthana's calm response suggest about how she sees Sahil's missed Fridays?
qa.a: It suggests she sees them as a common way brains picture the clean version of work, not as laziness, since her own bars were late too.

qa.q: Why is asking for two dates useful?
qa.a: The likely date keeps the hope, while the almost-certain date builds in a buffer, so others can plan on something real.

qa.q: How might Sahil have felt when the chart showed almost everyone was late?
qa.a: Sahil, who looked more embarrassed each Monday, may have felt relieved not to be singled out.

grounding: A new engineer watches a lead treat a teammate's repeated optimistic dates as a shared pattern and ask for two dates.

passage:
Week 1, Monday. Vikas told Sunaina the warehouse report would be ready Wednesday. On Friday he apologised; it would be Monday. Sunaina felt a flash of irritation and nearly wrote "lazy?" in her notes. Then she scrolled up. Prerna had slipped by three days last month. Sunaina herself had promised the budget "by the 10th" and sent it on the 16th.
Week 2, Thursday. At the team huddle, Sunaina said, "I've noticed we all guess short, me included. From now on, give me a range: earliest and latest." Vikas said, "Tuesday to the following Monday." Everyone laughed, but he wrote it down.
Week 4, Friday. The review sheet had three columns: estimate, range, actual. Most actual dates now fell inside the ranges. Vikas's report came in on the Thursday, right in the middle.

qa.q: When did Sunaina send the budget she had promised by the 10th?
qa.a: She sent it on the 16th.

qa.q: Why did Sunaina change her mind about writing 'lazy?' about Vikas?
qa.a: Her irritation faded when, scrolling up, she saw that Prerna and she herself had also slipped. She saw a shared habit, not one lazy person.

qa.q: Why did the review sheet with three columns work?
qa.a: Tracking estimate, range and actual showed whether the ranges were realistic, and most actual dates landed inside them.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel being asked for a range instead of being scolded?
qa.a: Vikas may feel relieved and more honest, joking with a wide range but writing it down and meeting it. 🙂

grounding: Over a month a lead notices everyone, herself included, guesses short, then asks for ranges and reviews past accuracy.

passage:
Saturday, 11 pm
Watched another video tonight: a guy who dropped out of college at nineteen and now owns a whole company. Three different toppers on the news said they only studied four hours a day. And that streamer everyone follows quit school in Class 11. So clearly school is optional if you're good.
I told Asif I might skip the coaching classes and just build my baking page instead. He said, "You only hear about the ones who made it." Classic Asif, always the wet blanket.
But... I tried to think of one person I actually know who left school and got famous. I couldn't. I only know them from videos.
Anyway. Sleeping on it.
Irawati

qa.q: What did Irawati tell Asif about the coaching classes?
qa.a: Irawati told Asif about maybe skipping the coaching classes to build a baking page instead.

qa.q: Why does school seem optional to Irawati tonight?
qa.a: Irawati feels hopeful and excited because every story on screen is someone who dropped out and succeeded, so the path looks easy and the many who failed never appear.

qa.q: What could Irawati do before deciding about the coaching classes?
qa.a: Irawati could look for people who tried the same path and didn't make it, and keep the classes while testing the baking page on the side.

qa.q: How does Asif see the videos Irawati is watching?
qa.a: Asif thinks they only show the ones who made it, so they give a false picture of how easy the path is.

grounding: A teenager concludes school is optional after seeing only dropouts who succeeded, missing the many who failed.

passage: Every time Suresh anna came home to Kothapalli from the city, he arrived in a new car and handed out sweets at the bus stand. Everyone knew he'd left school in Class 9. Darshan, fifteen, watched him from the tea shop and made up his mind. "School is a waste," he told his sister Urmila that night, while she checked his notebook by the light of the lantern. "Suresh anna left, and look at him." Urmila put the notebook down. "And Ramu? And the two Reddy boys? They left too." Darshan shrugged. He hadn't thought about them; nobody talked about them. Ramu worked at the brick kiln now. The Reddy boys had gone to the city and come back with nothing, and they never stood at the bus stand handing out sweets.

qa.q: What did Suresh anna do every time he came home?
qa.a: He arrived in a new car and handed out sweets at the bus stand.

qa.q: Why did Darshan decide school is a waste?
qa.a: Darshan felt impressed by Suresh anna's new car and sweets at the bus stand, while those who left and struggled were never talked about.

qa.q: What could Darshan ask before deciding to leave school?
qa.a: He could ask what happened to everyone who left, like Ramu and the Reddy boys, not just the one who came back rich.

qa.q: How does Urmila see Suresh anna's story differently?
qa.a: Urmila remembers Ramu and the Reddy boys too, so she sees Suresh anna as one success among several who struggled.

grounding: A village teenager decides school is pointless from one visible success, not seeing the dropouts who quietly failed.

passage: In Kasauli's narrow market, Mehak's aunt ran a small pickle stall, and Mehak, twenty and home for the holidays, had big plans for it. She'd been watching interviews with famous founders. They all woke at four, skipped breakfast, and said "never keep a fallback". So Mehak set her alarm for four, stopped eating before noon, and told her aunt to stop supplying the dhaba so they could go all in on online orders. Her cousin Anand, who ran the dhaba's kitchen, listened over chai. "Didn't the man with the pickle website in Solan do exactly that?" he asked. "He shut down last year." Mehak waved it off. The founders on her screen had done it and succeeded. The ones who'd done it and failed didn't give interviews.

qa.q: What did Mehak tell her aunt to stop doing?
qa.a: Mehak told her aunt to stop supplying the dhaba so they could go all in on online orders.

qa.q: Why does Mehak trust the founders' habits so completely?
qa.a: Every founder on her screen had those habits and succeeded, so the habits look like the cause, while those who failed stay unseen.

qa.q: What could Mehak do before changing the stall's business?
qa.a: She could look into sellers like the Solan man who tried the same thing and failed, and test online orders while keeping the dhaba supply.

qa.q: How might Mehak's aunt be affected if she stops supplying the dhaba?
qa.a: Her aunt could lose steady income from the dhaba because of habits copied from interviews.

grounding: A student copies famous founders' habits and plans, brushing aside a nearby example of someone with the same habits who failed.

passage: Felix had printed a list and taped it above his desk in the Munich flat: "Habits of Great Founders". Sleep five hours. Drop out when your idea takes off. Never listen to doubters. He'd got all of it from a bestselling book about famous startups. His flatmate Aiko, who studied statistics, read it while waiting for the kettle. "Who wrote down the habits of the founders who failed?" she asked. "Nobody writes books about them," said Felix. "Exactly," she said. "How many people sleep five hours and ignore doubters and still go broke?" Felix frowned. He thought of his cousin's food-delivery idea, which had eaten two years and all his savings. Same habits. No book. He didn't take the list down. But that night he slept eight hours.

qa.q: What was the title of the list above Felix's desk?
qa.a: Habits of Great Founders.

qa.q: Why did the list seem convincing to Felix?
qa.a: Felix felt inspired by a book about famous startups, where every example had the habits and the success together, making the habits look like the cause.

qa.q: What question from Aiko could Felix keep using?
qa.a: He could keep asking how many people did the same thing and still failed, before copying any habit from a success story.

qa.q: How does Aiko's statistics training shape the way she sees the list?
qa.a: Aiko looks for the missing group, the founders who failed, so she sees the list as one-sided rather than a recipe.

grounding: A student copies habits from successful founders until a flatmate asks about everyone with the same habits who failed.

passage: At the college incubation cell, Amandeep presented his plan for a campus laundry pickup service to the mentor panel. "We're following the founder playbook," he said. "Launch before it's ready, spend big on ads, skip the market research, like the famous ones did." Jatin, the final-year mentor on the panel, leaned forward. "How many campus startups has the cell funded in the last five years?" Amandeep didn't know. Jatin pulled up the list: forty-two. Three were still running. "Most of the other thirty-nine followed the same playbook," Jatin said. "You only know the three because they give talks at orientation." Amandeep stared at the screen. He had sat in those talks, taking notes. The other thirty-nine had never been invited.

qa.q: How many campus startups has the cell funded in the last five years?
qa.a: Forty-two, and three were still running.

qa.q: Why did the playbook feel like the right plan to Amandeep?
qa.a: Amandeep felt confident because he had only heard the three successful founders at orientation talks, so their habits seemed like the reason they won.

qa.q: What should Amandeep look at before launching?
qa.a: He should study why the other thirty-nine closed, and maybe do the market research the playbook told him to skip.

qa.q: How might the founders of the thirty-nine closed startups see the orientation talks?
qa.a: They might feel the talks give a lopsided picture, since they followed similar steps and were never invited to speak.

grounding: A student copies a famous founder playbook until a mentor shows most funded startups with the same habits failed.

passage:
Tuesday
The coaching institute's ad was everywhere today: "95% of our students placed!" and a wall of smiling faces. Lokesh has already paid the deposit. I almost did too.
But at the counselling desk I asked: 95% of whom? Turns out it's 95% of students who finished and sat the final test. How many joined? The man at the desk got vague. Lokesh's senior told us half the batch dropped out by month three. So maybe it's more like half of half.
Not saying it's bad. Maybe it's great. But before I pay anything, I'm going to find five people who joined and didn't finish, and ask them what happened.
Shankar

qa.q: What did the coaching institute's ad say?
qa.a: 95% of our students placed, with a wall of smiling faces.

qa.q: Why did Shankar ask '95% of whom?'
qa.a: Shankar felt doubtful that the smiling faces showed everyone, suspecting they were only those who finished, and wanted to know about everyone who joined.

qa.q: What makes Shankar's plan a sensible one?
qa.a: Talking to five people who joined and didn't finish shows the whole group, including the missing ones, before any money is paid.

qa.q: How might Lokesh feel after hearing Shankar's questions?
qa.a: Lokesh, who already paid the deposit, might feel uneasy or defensive, but also prompted to ask what happened to the dropouts.

grounding: Someone in their mid-twenties asks what the full batch looked like, including dropouts, before trusting a course's success figure.

passage: At the panchayat meeting in Dhanauri, a seed dealer pointed to three farmers in the front row. "All three used our new wheat seed, and all three doubled their harvest!" Heads nodded. Shreya, the young agriculture extension worker, raised her hand. "How many farmers in the block bought this seed last season?" The dealer hesitated. "Around forty." "And the other thirty-seven?" Nazia, a farmer at the back, called out, "My field had the same seed. Half of it failed." Two more hands went up. Shreya kept her voice friendly. "Maybe it's a good seed. But before the panchayat praises it, let's hear from all forty, and check whose fields had canal water." The dealer's smile tightened. The three in the front row shifted in their seats.

qa.q: How many farmers bought the new seed last season, according to the dealer?
qa.a: Around forty.

qa.q: Why did Shreya ask about the other thirty-seven?
qa.a: Shreya felt doubtful that the three in the front row told the whole story, and wanted to see the whole group before praising the seed.

qa.q: What does Shreya propose the panchayat do next?
qa.a: Hear from all forty farmers and check whose fields had canal water before praising the seed.

qa.q: How might Nazia feel when Shreya's question gives her a chance to speak?
qa.a: Nazia, whose field half failed, may feel relieved that her loss finally counts in the story.

grounding: A young extension worker asks about all the farmers who used a seed, not just the three winners, before it is praised.

passage:
Dear Farhan,
Nanaji took me around old Lucknow on Sunday. At every haveli he'd tap a wall and say, "See? Two hundred years. Today's buildings won't last twenty." I nodded, because the carved doors really are beautiful.
But as an architect, something kept bugging me. We were only walking past the old buildings that are still standing. What about the ones from the same time that cracked, flooded, or were pulled down a century ago? They're not on the tour. They're parking lots now.
So maybe old builders weren't all better. Maybe we only get to see their best work.
I didn't say this to Nanaji. He was so happy. But I keep wondering which of our buildings people will be admiring two hundred years from now.
Ganga

qa.q: What did Nanaji say at every haveli?
qa.a: See? Two hundred years. Today's buildings won't last twenty.

qa.q: What was Ganga thinking while walking past the havelis?
qa.a: Ganga realised they were only seeing the old buildings still standing, not the ones from the same time that fell or were pulled down.

qa.q: How could Ganga share this idea with Nanaji kindly?
qa.a: Ganga could admire the carved doors with Nanaji and gently ask what happened to buildings from his childhood that are gone.

qa.q: How does Nanaji experience the walk?
qa.a: Nanaji is proud and happy, seeing the standing havelis as proof that the old ways were better.

grounding: A young architect hears that old buildings were better made and notes that only the durable ones are still around to be seen.

passage: My uncle says it every Sunday lunch: "Old songs had soul. Today's songs are noise." And honestly, Ganga, the old playlist he puts on is gorgeous. But here's what I figured out, working at the radio station. I'm Tushar, I handle the archive. We have boxes of records from the sixties, hundreds of film songs nobody has played in forty years. Some are fine, most are forgettable, a few are truly terrible. They never made it into anyone's playlist. So when my uncle compares his top fifty old songs with whatever new song comes on the radio, it's not a fair fight. The weak old ones have already been forgotten. Give today's songs forty years, and the best of them will sound like soul too.

qa.q: What does Tushar handle at the radio station?
qa.a: Tushar handles the archive.

qa.q: What does Tushar think the boxes of old records show?
qa.a: Tushar realised most old songs were forgettable and simply dropped away, and seems amused that only the best reach the uncle's playlist.

qa.q: How could Tushar test the idea with the uncle over lunch?
qa.a: Tushar could play a few random songs from the archive boxes and see whether the uncle still hears soul in all of them. 🙂

qa.q: Why might Tushar's uncle feel so sure old songs were better?
qa.a: The uncle only hears the top fifty that survived, so the old era sounds full of gems next to random new songs.

grounding: A young archivist hears that old songs were better and notes that only the best old songs are still being played.

passage: I'm Pranav, and I was at the office farewell when Mr Rawat started on his favourite topic. "In our time, steel almirahs lasted forty years. Everything today breaks in two." Most of us nodded politely. Vidya, who joined last year as an engineer, smiled and said, "Sir, your almirah lasted. But how many from that factory rusted in five years and went to the kabadiwala?" Mr Rawat laughed. "Those were cheap ones." "Exactly," Vidya said gently. "The cheap ones are gone, so we only meet the good ones." I watched Mr Rawat pause, fork halfway to his mouth. I don't know if he agreed. But later I heard him telling his neighbour about his brother's old scooter that broke down every week, which he'd clearly forgotten until then.

qa.q: What did Mr Rawat say about steel almirahs?
qa.a: In our time, steel almirahs lasted forty years, and everything today breaks in two.

qa.q: What might Vidya have been thinking when asking about the kabadiwala?
qa.a: Vidya seemed to be thinking that the rusted almirahs had disappeared, so only the lasting ones were left to admire.

qa.q: What made Vidya's way of raising the point work?
qa.a: Vidya smiled, called him Sir and asked a question instead of contradicting him, so Mr Rawat could think about it without losing face.

qa.q: How might remembering his brother's scooter change Mr Rawat's view?
qa.a: It may remind him that plenty of old things were poorly made too, and simply aren't around any more.

grounding: A colleague watches a young engineer point out that only durable old almirahs survive, answering an elder's old-is-better talk.

passage:
"Ammi, everyone in my class has a spinning top with lights. Everyone!"
Zeenat looked up from the sewing machine. "Faraz, last month you said spinning tops were for babies."
"That was before. Now Mohit and Varun and the whole back bench have them. They have battles at lunch."
"And you want to battle?"
"I want to be in the battles."
"Do you like spinning tops?"
Faraz thought about it. "Not really. My kite is better. But nobody flies kites now."
"So you want a toy you don't like?"
"I want the toy they like. If I have it, I can sit with them."
Zeenat stopped the machine. "Tell me about lunch these days, beta."
Faraz looked at his feet. "I sit with my kite book."

qa.q: What does Faraz say is better than a spinning top?
qa.a: Faraz says his kite is better.

qa.q: Why does Faraz want a toy he doesn't even like?
qa.a: He wants to be in the lunch battles and sit with the others, so being included matters more to him than his own taste. 🥺

qa.q: How could Zeenat support Faraz beyond buying the top?
qa.a: She could keep asking about lunch, help him find one friend to share his kite with, and talk about joining in without pretending.

qa.q: What is Zeenat noticing when she stops the sewing machine?
qa.a: Zeenat notices this isn't really about a toy; Faraz seems lonely at lunch and wants a way in.

grounding: A boy wants the spinning top his whole class has, though he prefers kites, because having it means he can sit with them.

passage: I'm Tejas, and this year I did a strange thing. In Class 5, everyone started collecting cricket sticker cards from the shop near school. I don't even like cricket; I like drawing birds. But every break, the whole class sat in a circle swapping cards, and I stood outside it. So I spent all my Diwali money on sticker packs and learned every player's name. I even told Vinita didi that birds were boring now. She stared and said, "Who is this boy, and where's my brother?" The funny part is, inside the circle I was happy. But at home I missed my bird notebook. Now I keep both. I swap cards at school, and I draw birds at home, secretly.

qa.q: What did Tejas spend all his Diwali money on?
qa.a: He spent all his Diwali money on sticker packs.

qa.q: Why did Tejas say birds were boring now?
qa.a: Tejas felt left out standing outside the swapping circle, so he began acting as if he liked what the group liked.

qa.q: What could help Tejas stop keeping his birds secret?
qa.a: He could bring his bird notebook to school once, or find one classmate who also likes drawing, so he doesn't have to hide it.

qa.q: How does Vinita didi experience her brother's change?
qa.a: Vinita didi is startled, as if he has become someone else, because she knows how much he loves drawing birds.

grounding: A boy buys sticker cards and claims to find birds boring so he can join his class's swapping circle.

passage:
Class 3B observation note, Ms Salma, Thursday
This week slime has taken over the class. Almost every child brings a tub. Kiran, who last term refused to touch finger paint because it felt "yucky", arrived on Monday with the biggest tub of all. At break he stood with the slime group, squeezing it and wiping his hands on his shorts every few seconds, face scrunched. When Divya asked if he liked it, he said, "Everyone likes it," not "I like it." He smiled most when the others let him sit in their circle, not when he played with the slime.
What I did: at story time, I asked each child to share one thing they love that nobody else in class does. Kiran said his clay dinosaurs. Two children asked to see them tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Kiran say when Divya asked if he liked slime?
qa.a: He said, 'Everyone likes it,' not 'I like it.'

qa.q: What does Kiran's scrunched face with the slime suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he doesn't enjoy the slime at all and brings it because sitting in the group's circle matters more to him.

qa.q: Why was Ms Salma's story-time question a good move?
qa.a: It let Kiran share his clay dinosaurs, showing him he can be included for what he really likes.

qa.q: How might the two children who asked to see the dinosaurs see Kiran now?
qa.a: They may see him as someone with an interesting hobby, not just another child with a tub of slime. 🙂

grounding: A teacher notes a boy who dislikes sticky things bringing slime to fit in, and helps him share his real interest.
